key_insight: A gut microbiome-derived risk score built from 28 microbial species was associated with a higher future risk of cancer diagnosis years before onset.
clinical_relevance: This suggests stool-based microbiome profiling could help identify people at elevated cancer risk for earlier risk stratification, though it is not ready for clinical use on its own.
method: Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool samples from 5,997 participants in population cohorts.
Built a microbiome risk score using 28 microbial species and tested association with incident cancer over up to 10 years.
Validated performance in independent cancer case-control and population-based cohorts.
evidence_signal: Higher microbiome risk scores were associated with incident cancer in follow-up (adjusted HR per 1-SD increase, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.44-1.82; P=1.54e-15) and also separated cancer cases from controls in external datasets.
watch_item: Associations do not prove causality, and the score needs further validation and calibration before any screening or clinical decision-making use.
paper_title: A gut microbiome-derived risk score is associated with future cancer development
